p:
I do know where to find you. I probably find you more than you want me to. But thank you both for your thoughtful questions. And Chair– and Director, we'll try to not pain you too much as you're under the weather. Just taking a step back to headcount. So MOCS FY26 budgeted headcount is for 246 positions, which I believe includes 10 positions at MONS, the Mayor's Office of Nonprofit Services, and 13 positions at the MWBE office. So taking those out, our understanding is that MOCS currently has 179 of 223 positions filled. That's a vacancy rate of almost 20 percent. I think you testified to 51 vacancies. Our numbers were 44, so, in that ballpark. We did a review of those vacancies and found that the highest vacancy rates were in the business optimization, infotech, and strategic initiatives, budget codes. Could you explain to us kind of what those units primarily do?

Why are we seeing higher vacancy rates in those units in particular?

Thank you so much, uh, for, for the question, Chair. And also, just— I have— I can't let it go, but to your commentary on Council Member Stevens, I think you're exactly right that the grant pilot will free— if it's successful, and we're very optimistic that will be successful, and it frees up capacity, it'll allow the city agencies to do more thoughtful competitive procurements, which is something that we are very eager to also have like as a benefit from the grant pilot. But, onto your question. So thank you for honing in on this particular issue. And I think, you know, the numbers may be like off one or two, but I think generally we're aligned. So I can speak about MOCS's staffing plan and the positions that– the team members we have and then the vacancies we have. And then also talk more about the teams that have the vacancies. You'll have to forgive me that I'm not the— I don't have the underpinning of like the structure, the budget– the, the budget codes that would align directly with the teams. But so let me– I'll talk about it from the way that I understand it.
Right.

So you're right that ballpark we've got about, you know, 200 team members and then we've got vacancies predominantly in three teams. We've got vacancies in our procurement operations team, which our procurement operations team covers both our team members who are working week to week with our agencies and project managing and tracking and ensuring compliance with procurement. And then we've also got our financial taskforce– our financials team members that also includes our payment task force members. And so, That is a large team and we do see a number of vacancies there. And then the other team that we see vacancies is our tech team. Our tech team– our tech team is very large relative to our overall size. And so we will see some vacancies there. The other area that we see our vacancies are in our General Counsel's office, but our General Counsel's office is larger than what you think like a general counsel, like legal office. It– they do things such as compliance. They do things ensuring vendor integrity. They do things– Local Law 34 compliance, which is on the pay-to-play, the lobbyist database. And so, you know,

those are the three teams that we see the most vacancies. So to drill down, let me talk first about the procurement operations. I'll share– I'll share, Chair, that we recently did a convening of the agency ACOs at the start of this new administration, this year one, to do a little bit of sharing and thinking about procurement and really to dig into some pain points. And staffing came up as a pain point. And, I'll say that agency staffing, that's right, yes, in procurement shops. But as we've shared, you know, the procurement ecosystem includes procurement, but then also legal and then also budget. And so there are vacancies, you know, within those respective teams. So what can I say that like attributes to some of that vacancy and those staffing pain points? The City of New York, as we all know, is subject to civil service. The civil service– you know, anybody who's read The Power Broker knows that the civil service is very complex. And, you know, for civil service that oversees particular titles, procurement titles are included. So, we've got procurement analyst and procurement– other procurement professionals there. And recruiting, as part of that process is something that requires time and effort. And so I will say that

that is something that we are in these beginning months very focused on sort of like getting under the hood on to really understand how we operate within those confines. For tech, I will say that the City of New York in its recruitment retention of tech resources and tech talent, it is uniquely positioned because we are competing with major tech organizations like Google, like Meta and those tech– that tech talent has the ability to just— it's just the reality– be compensated at a different scale than the City of New York could compensate our tech resources. So our— but what sort of grounds us when we recruit for tech resources is this public service. So our tech, we really– our tech recruiting really– we look for individuals who are looking to come into the city, be part of something bigger than themselves, and to contribute to something as large-scale as Passport and the large scale that it supports for procurement and contracting in the City of New York. And then for– you know, I would say, we see less vacancies in our General Counsel team, the very large General Counsel team and the myriad of responsibilities that they carry out. But we do see some vacancies there, and I think that that is just,

I think natural, in any organization. There's going to be, vacancy— vacancies, and there's going to be attrition. And it's just– I think it's just to be expected. So that's a little bit of an overview.

Yeah, that's insightful and really helpful. Thank you for such a detailed overview for us. I think, you know, Council Member Stevens and I were talking about this on the way in, that, you know, when MOCS has inadequate capacity, it affects the work of every agency. Just like when the Contracts Division at the Law Department has inadequate capacity, it affects and slows down the work of every agency. And so we want to make sure that you're resourced properly, that you have the adequate headcount you need so that every agency is able to procure the goods and services that they need to support New Yorkers. You know, it doesn't surprise me that we've had challenges in the tech division. You know, that's, I imagine, a persistent issue over time. I am more surprised about the Payments Division. Could you give us a little bit more insight there? This is a newer division. They– and they're overseeing budget readiness and they're overseeing, kind of– they're reviewing invoices to

make sure that those are being paid properly. This is really important, and I think an area where we can be doing more, where MOCS can be doing even more to ensure that agencies are really on the ball. Can you give more specifics on how many headcount, are in that unit? How many are vacant? And is there anything we can do to be helpful in making sure that that unit is properly supported?

Thank you, Council Member— or thank you, Chairman, for honing in on this. So our financials team that includes our payment task force, we've got, um, seven team members overseeing payments for all of the City of New York.
Seven?
Seven, yes. We've got– we've got one vacancy. So we've got six. I will say, as I spoke about in my testimony a bit, it is new for MOCS to be in the invoice accountability space.
Right.

It is a result of the– in many ways, the technology pulling in these processes and then opening up the transparency for how agencies are performing relative to their invoice

accountability. I want to– within the last year, forgive me for not knowing, but–
Through your leadership?

Yes. Yeah. But I certainly– we did, I did this with my predecessor. Yes. So, I would say that the city as a whole likely may be experiencing the entry level or the entry point for a city employee, probably needs to be– are we appropriately compensating them? Are we– is it the right skill set? But for our financials– for our financials team, we've been very fortunate that we've– beside the one vacancy now, we've been pretty fully staffed since its creation. And I'll say also that I joked about this in our last hearing, that once we get them in, get them trained up, a lot of agencies like to recruit them. But that is a healthy, healthy thing, and it's something that we lean into. It's something that we understand as part of the process and having MOCS train them and get them familiar with operating within public service is something that we welcome. And then once we deploy them to the agencies, they're– they have the relationships. They have the resources. And so,

yeah, it's something that we've had a lot of success with. You know, we've gotten those resources. We've been able to hire those resources, and we've been able to send those resources out into what we call– like deploy them, so to speak.

Well, that's great. And I think, you know, I think you deserve credit for creating this unit and, you know, hopefully it's a unit that we can see grow and can help support agencies to make sure that there is crisp accountability on budget readiness and invoice processing so that folks are getting paid. Our review found that there were currently 15 positions on the NYC jobs website for MOCS, you know, for MOCS openings, not including interns and things like that and the MONs and MWB openings. Are you able to give insight into, you know, if we've got three times as many vacancies as that roughly, why would— are we— why would we not have postings up for more positions? And you may not be familiar with exactly—
[interposing] Chairman, Yes, I'm so sorry. I'm not following 100 percent. Yeah.

Well, I'm— if there's only— if we're looking at about 44 vacancies,

give or take, and there's only 15 positions that are posted for on the website, is that because other positions, it's just, we're waiting for lists on civil service and different things, and that may explain why we're not seeing active hiring efforts for more of the vacant positions?

I see. I see what you're asking. Yes. So, I'll say this. In this particular season that we're in and when it comes to the recruitment efforts, we are in active conversations with both City Hall and OMB about how we are prioritizing and turning those vacancies external.
Right.
And, um, it is a series of negotiations and conversations. And so that may be why you'll see more– less postings up than we have vacancies shown on our– on some of the budget documents.

And I should acknowledge Council Member Gale Brewer. Thank you for being with us. And Council Member Brewer, whenever you'd like to jump in for questions, just let us know. The mayor announced with prelim that he was eliminating about half of the vacancies that

currently exist. It's been a little hazy for us, and I think this is at every budget hearing— agency heads are getting asked to similar question of like, how is this information being conveyed down? We know savings plans were submitted earlier this week, last— this week, this week, last week, in the last few days. The 20th, last week, Friday. Time is a flat circle. Last week. And that, you know, I imagine Director Soliman will be sharing more insight with us tomorrow at the OMB budget hearing. But have you received guidance on– of the 44-odd vacancies, how many of those positions are being eliminated as of yet, or is that an ongoing conversation? Can you share any insight with us there?

Candidly, I'll say it's an ongoing conversation. Certainly we were– we understand where we are fiscally. We just, you know, just as a New Yorker, we— I understand. And just as I mentioned in these very early months in a brand new administration to sort of look at our resources, our, our staffing levels and our capacity. This is I think the work that we're in the midst of right now. And so we have had conversations with OMB about what that looks like in particular to MOCs. What it would mean

in terms of, you know, OTPS savings, vacancy reductions. Nothing is finalized. We're just— we're very much in those conversations.

There's going to be a need for efficiencies everywhere. You know, it's worth noting that, you know, after multiple years of cuts under Mayor Adams, you know, this council— the previous council pushed to restore headcount to the 245/246 level, which is where we had been before these rounds of budget cuts, you know, at the end of the de Blasio administration. And I hope that we don't see a significant reduction in MOCS headcount because, as I said, it has an impact on the work that every agency does. And I don't want to see procurements held up because we don't have enough folks at MOCS to review and provide support and assistance. Council Member Brewer is ready. I'm gonna just ask one more question on this topic, and then I'll shut up and pass it over to Council Member Brewer. Is attrition– can you speak to the attrition rate that we've seen at MOCS if you have that data handy? What we saw last year, I think what was testified to in FY25 prelim, was an attrition rate of 19 percent with high attrition rates within the

technology unit for reasons that we've discussed. Are you seeing persistently high attrition? Do you have that data for this past year?

Chairman, I would want to be specific in— I want to– just memory, I think we've stayed level, but I will follow up with you about that. And one of the things I will say is some of the attrition is sort of what I spoke about earlier is some of the agencies sort of like reaching from us and pulling.
[inaudible] Totally.
Yeah.

No, it’s– I mean, we've seen it a lot with OMB over the years of like really talented people on task force at OMB or unit heads at OMB getting plucked off to run, you know, fiscal office– you know, run, be in charge of the financial offices at agencies, and it's great. I mean, these are folks who clearly have the expertise to do it, and for your folks to be going over to run procurement shops and support fiscal teams at agencies, it makes a lot of sense. And agencies often pay higher, and so there's a double incentive, and probably they work less hard. So, you know, for all

of those different reasons, you understand why those trajectories happen. But we want to make sure that we're, you know, celebrating your team and celebrating, you know, the good work that MOCS is doing. So if there are ways that the Council can do that and support if they're– you know, give citations or recognize, you know, folks who go above and beyond to really make our system work better. We're always happy to be partners in that effort. Let me pass it over to Council Member Brewer, and then I'll keep going.

Okay. I mean, I have very few questions, because I was next door, but I guess one of the issues is you have said in the past, and I think correctly, that the small contracts are hard, you know, and so I'm just wondering– you got the small ones that the Council often gives you and then you have the larger ones that come from agencies, etcetera. So my question is, is there something we can do, or is it the same process and they're all the same, or is there something that could be helpful to you in some of the smaller contracts? Because there are a lot of them. And I just wanted to know, because they're often the

smaller groups too, and so they have more challenges on their end. So, is there anything– I don't know if it's a longer life cycle, even though it seems to be year to year to year. I don't know. I'm just asking to see if there's anything we can do for the smaller dollar figures that are probably as time-consuming maybe as some of the larger ones, but not for a lot of money.

Thank you, Council Member, for the question. It— so we're in the midst of a collaboration with the City Council right now on those discretionary contracts that tend to be lower dollar value to our nonprofits, to our community-based organizations that end up being just retroactive. Like, right out the gate, they're already late.
Right.
The services have already been provided, and the money often just like catches up with them. Like, you know, maybe a year after the services have already been provided.
Yes.

So, we are in year one of the grant pilot with a really small cohort, about 100

providers, where we looked at the very– the traditional procurement process, and rather than treating them as contracts that go through the procurement process–
[interposing] Grants.
We treat them as grants, exactly.
I remember that pilot.

Yes. Yes. And so we're very- so we're proud to be able to speak about the 100 in that cohort. We looked at the cycle time from grant signature to payment, and it was about four months versus oftentimes like over a year.
Yeah.
And in addition to the money faster, there's less steps and then less time. And so we are– we're planning on scaling that up for FY27 and we'll increase the cohort from 100 to 800.
Okay.
And that's something–
[interposing] How do you decide the 800? Is it random? Is it something that has a consistent—
[interposing] They're all from District 33.
They're all from my district.
It's something—
[interposing] They want the pilot.
It's something that we're in conversations with the Council about, about who gets into that cohort.

Okay, because I assume— how many are there of this magnitude approximately? The, you know, the ones at the Council? I assume there are others besides just the City Council, but it's mostly the city council.
It's all city council.
All city council. Okay, how many do you have? Some said from 800 to– I should know, but it looks like it's thousands.

Council Member, if you give me one moment, I can probably tell you. I don't know

it off the top of my head, but let me see if I can tell you how many.
I mean, I've looked at all those lists.
It would be organizations that receive no more than $20,000 to $25,000 from a single city agency via council discretionary funding.
That's right.
That's the— just to be clear about the—
[interposing] So that would be the number that we're looking at.
That's a yes. I was just clarifying.
That's helpful.
Yeah.
Because 800 is a small portion of that, I would assume. Because there's– I mean, I give out many more than 800.
Yes. So for FY26, there were 10,000 awards.
Okay.
10,000 total city council awards, not just that fit that description of per— that received– organizations that received no more than $20,000, $25,000.
That's right, the whole–
Well, that's– so that's a manageable number then for the future.
10,000, yes. But the 10,000 includes, you know, our very large social service organizations that receive–
[interposing] So what we're saying though is that 800 is gonna cover quite a few of what we're talking about.
You know, it’s eight percent, whatever it is. We're getting there.
Okay.
But we should be doing more.
Yes.
We should– you know, the three-year–
[interposing] I'd love to see the whole list be covered. The one that fit into the criteria.

Yes, I mean the– so, you know, the large social service organizations that have contracts with the city or that receive council initiative funding for $50,000 or $100,000 or more, they're not gonna benefit from this grant pilot.
Right. It's the smaller ones.

These are the small neighborhood groups that just receive a little, you know, five from you or five from me or five from a couple council members. So, and you know, as for the nonprofits and for the agencies, they spend as much time on the $5,000 grant as for the $500,000 grant.
And my staff spends the other amount of time trying to help them.
Yes, exactly.
So I'm very aware of it.
Mine, too.
The other question, I see you do this, but do you meet with non— you said last time, I think you meet with nonprofits to figure out what their issues are.
Yes.
Is that like quarterly or how often, or is it just when it's needed?
So we have a few different ways we reach the nonprofits. We certainly– we have trainings. We do webinar. We do live trainings. We do webinars. We do–
[interposing] Correct.

what we call like coffee hour, like one-on-one. And actually, I was recently in the Bronx with, Council Member Stevens where she does a convening of nonprofits in her district. And so we'll certainly do it on ad hoc.
Okay.
Yes.

All right. And then I know you talked about technology. So what is– is there a cost to the amount of technology that you use or it's not broken down in that way in terms of the– because it is incredibly helpful to you, obviously, to have the best. Is it a program that you're using or used by the state? Is there some

other sort of sister agencies that you can look at in terms of doing a sort of– a MOCS elsewhere, or are you on your own in terms of the technology?
So, MOCS oversees the procurement technology.
Correct, Right. But I'm just didn’t know, like, does the state have similar technology? Does California have similar technology, etcetera?
I understand–
[interposing] With that size.
So, Councilmember, we are unique in our scale. There's really no one— there's no city like us, right? And the comparable public sector equivalent would be the state of California.
Correct.
And how much they procure and contract.
Correct, yep.

You mentioned New York State. We are in partnership with New York State, and actually they are learning from us a bit about, moving their processes into– in a digital— from a

paper to a digital way. And also the way that they buy is a little different than the way that we buy, and so it's not going to be a one-to-one. But there's a lot that we can gain by having partnerships with the State of New York and how their– what technology they're using for their contracting. And so we have those conversations all the time. And so, but you mentioned Passport, and maybe if I could give you like a little bit of overview.
Yeah. No, I know Passport.
Yes. On Passport. So Passport is a software, right?
Yes.

It's a software and it's– there are two vendors who sup— who give us access to the software and maintain the software. So Passport is an Ivalua– it's a Ivalua product. The City of New York through MOCS pays about $2.5 million every year to be able to access that software.
Yep.

And then Accenture is our systems integrator and they provide us a lot of support as we tailor the Ivalua Passport product to

the specifics of how New York City buys things. And we spend about $7.5 million per year. So in total, it's about $10 to $11 million that we're–
[interposing] Okay.
that it costs to maintain Passport.
Right. And that's basically the software and the— that you need in order technology-wise in order to do what you need to do.
Yes.
My friends at Accenture are very happy. All right. Thank you very much.
Thank you, Council Member.

Thank you so much, Council Member Brewer, for your always insightful questions. One more just headcount capacity-oriented question for me was– is, do you believe MOCS has enough capacity to efficiently process the indirect cost rate directive and COLA adjustments?

Chair, I would welcome a further conversation. Some of the indirect cost rate

work and the cost of living adjustment work is actually in the agencies. So the agency– and I would have to do a little bit more to be able to respond very comprehensively. What MOCS does do is that we oversee, in collaboration with OMB, and also– So let me break it apart. So for ICR, for ICR, it is a MOCS team, our nonprofit team, that is overseeing the ICR process. Vendors submit, you know, their ICR rate, and then it follows along and it gets approved and then it gets actioned, right? And so our team is working with the agencies to make sure that that is implemented. And also setting– really thinking about, because we know that this is a pain point, is, is the process, um, attuned to what is effective? So we've, we've had some recent changes on the, on the ICR policy and also what is required when. So that's on the ICR. On COLA, COLA is something that we, work closely with OMB, and it is really a really– a really OMB agency exercise for COLA to make sure that the cost of living adjustments are making their way into the contracts, whether it's through an allowance adjustment or whether it's a contract amendment. Right. So it's a little bit of like a multifaceted

and I would welcome having a follow-up conversation about this.

Great. That's helpful. Um, I look forward to that follow-up conversation. It'd be helpful to go into it a little more detail. Ah, on agency staffing, you mentioned this little bit of your ACO convening from earlier in the year, and we discussed this a bit at our last hearing, and I understand that MOCS is not currently tracking kind of headcount at agencies, uh, in their contracting, probably fiscal offices and legal offices too. But we're, you know, are there any ideas for how we could track that information better? Or should that information be reported into MOCS so that you have better insight into agency capacity?
Chair, I certainly, through our conversations, this is like certain– I think is worthwhile exploring and I would welcome exploring it in partnership.
Great.

I think what I, what I can share is here was an exercise where we just started with a survey. We started with the— it was, it was a voluntary survey and it was really just to, um, gauge

where staffing levels were within the, those respective shops that you, that you listed. And then once we have a little bit more of the data, I think, that will, that will provide some grounding for what we do with it and some, um, patterns maybe we can observe or recommendations that we can make. Um, and then also sort of maybe crosswalking that with the, the output, the, the contract volume, the contract dollars, the complexity of the contracts. It’s, uh, yeah, an exercise that I would welcome.

Either rnGreat. To do in partnership. We would welcome that. And I, you know, Council Member Brewer is here. I know that the new DCAS commissioner is really focused on how do we improve our civil service systems and streamline hiring. I am at— I was sorry to miss your budget hearing, but I imagine that was one of the main things that she discussed a week ago Friday. And we'd love to help prioritize, you know, procurement staff, fiscal staff, and to make sure that agencies are, you know, have the ability to swiftly hire for those positions as much as possible. And, you know, welcome the opportunity to think about ways that we can track that together and, and hold agencies

accountable. Wy don't I do some Passport-related questions, and then I'll kick it back over to Councilmember Stevens. So, FY27 Preliminary Plan is $9.5 million less than FY26 at Adopted. The council had pushed hard for, you know, well over $7 million essentially in Passport-related support. My understanding is that the main improvements for this funding will allow for vendors to submit invoices while budget mods are in progress. Are there— we don't have additional funds set aside for FY27 for further Passport upgrades. Everybody has a lot of feelings about Passport, a lot of feelings. That was maybe the nicest way I could say it. God, yes, according to Councilmember Brewer. Are there additional improvements that you've been considering for Passport that we should be looking to try to fund in this upcoming budget that would be helpful?

Thank you for the question, Chair. Yes. Recognizing and appreciating so much of the procurement process that the city has now is, you know, has made just so many leaps from where it was previously. We went from a paper-based system to a digital system in a very short amount of time. And as I mentioned in my testimony, everybody's in.

Everybody's in, and previously not everybody was in, and everybody's in for procurement and contracting. And even before that vendor enrollment and then also for financials, for budgeting, for payment. But as I also mentioned in my testimony, there– the technology is– was purchased and it was developed and purchased a number of years ago. And technology is just— technology just evolved so quickly. And I think that there is more to certainly to think about and– about the technology in the coming months. And certainly, you said it very nicely about the very known— yes, feelings about Passport, about, you know, the system performance and the user— the usability. That's not something that we're shying away from. It's something that we have really tried to focus about, you know, stabilization of the system. And then also, this happened in the prior budget cycle. We did receive additional service desk team members at MOCS to help with our vendors who are trying to do business with the City of New York and in Passport and providing them a little bit more of a touchpoint, as they– as they're trying to, you know, get their contracts through. I would welcome further conversations on Passport. And just to look back, the- you're right

that you'll see from FY26 to FY27, there was a– there was more money in FY27 budget for MOCS to support a technology improvement, which is the, as you mentioned, the invoicing and payment. And in the– there were some funds also for the vendor reports that I spoke about in my testimony. So, technology, like so many things, it requires— it requires resources and it requires keeping up with what's modern. And, um, it's like anything, like, you know? We don't walk around with the same phone that we did 10 years ago. And similarly, a car, we don't like— like– if we're lucky, maybe we get like 10 years out of a car, but things have a life. And so, yeah, I would welcome further conversations.

Some of the suggestions we've heard from agencies in our conversations around Passport improvements are simultaneous law and OMB review, improving the bulk upload template and team setups, improving interfaces— the interface between PIP and Passport. So I think we're certainly getting lots of suggestions of ways in which the technology could be better tailored to meet the needs of city agencies, and I'm sure vendor— and our nonprofit partners and

vendors. And I think we're happy to push, you know, for resources in the upcoming budget for areas that you think would, would have the greatest impact. Do you– do you have a mechanism to kind of collect that agency feedback on, like, ways Passport can be better?

Yes, yes. From time to time we have, uh, convened the agencies for a little bit of a wish list, so to speak. We did it most recently with our construction agencies, and we did some cataloging of wish lists and then we did some, you know, just what we call like requirements gathering. And then we asked– we did it with, within MOCS, but we also asked some of our contracted resources, Accenture, to help estimate what something like that would cost. And that's actually how we– that was the– that activity is how we got the the piece of functionality that we are building now, which is, that what we are calling Passport Release seven, that's on the payments, um, and financials. It's something that, um– yes,we have to expend some attention to focus on. Yeah, look, I, we had heard through the grapevine in our conversations with agencies that the construction agencies ask for the

sun, the moon, and the stars. And, I guess it's, it's the role of agencies to make asks, and for you as well to, to make your asks. And you know, obviously we're in a tough fiscal moment right now, and so, you know, this may or may not be the opportunity where we can make new investments, but it's certainly helpful for us to understand what the shortlist looks like for you of like most critical passport improvements so that we can try and help advocate for them together. I guess with that, and then I'll pass it to Council Member Stevens— are there any new needs that MOCS has identified that you'd like to share with us today? Um, we're happy for you to come back to us in Exec if that's a— I guess we probably won't have an Exec hearing, will we? Probably not. No. So this— you won't be coming back to us in Exec. Sorry, or maybe not sorry. The– so are there any things you'd like to, while we give you an opportunity on the record?

For this season, we have not advocated for any new needs. But, Chair, I welcome the partnership and we hope to, you know, do this in the years to come. So, I hope to stay very close and in coordination with you about our new needs requests.
Right. Council Member Stevens?

Yeah, I just have a quick question. It's also related to Passport. We've heard from some organizations that the process and information requested may be different depending on the agency. With the creation of Passport, one of the goals were to streamline the contracting process for organizations and agency. Does each contracting agency have the same process to register, and reimburse contracts, or is this process and information being requested different from each agency? And if so, why?
